blocks.text: Have you ever wondered how a computer decides which part of a complex expression to evaluate first? Understanding operator precedence and associativity is key to mastering this.

blocks.markdown: In programming, expressions are combinations of values, variables, operators, and function calls that are evaluated to produce another value. Operators are special symbols or keywords that tell the compiler or interpreter to perform specific operations. Understanding how expressions are evaluated is crucial for writing correct and efficient code.

blocks.title: Operator Precedence
blocks.text: Operator precedence determines the order in which different operators in an expression are evaluated. Operators with higher precedence are evaluated before operators with lower precedence.

blocks.title: Associativity
blocks.text: Associativity defines the order in which operators of the same precedence level are evaluated. Most operators are left-associative, meaning they are evaluated from left to right.

blocks.caption: In this expression, multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so it is evaluated first, resulting in 3 + (4 \times 2) = 3 + 8 = 11.

blocks.title: Evaluating an Expression

steps.text: Identify the operators and their precedence: exponentiation (^), multiplication (\times), division (/), addition (+), and subtraction (-).
Evaluate the highest precedence operator first: $2^2 = 4$.
Next, evaluate the multiplication and division from left to right: $3 \times 4 = 12$ and $4 / 2 = 2$.
Finally, evaluate the addition and subtraction from left to right: $5 + 12 - 2 = 15$.

blocks.answer: The result of the expression is 15.

blocks.markdown: Comparison operators are used to compare two values. They include `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, and `>=`. Logical operators, such as `&&` (AND), `||` (OR), and `!` (NOT), are used to build compound conditions.

blocks.title: Using Comparison and Logical Operators

steps.text: Evaluate each comparison separately: $3 > 2$ is true, and $5 < 10$ is true.
Combine the results using the AND operator: true AND true results in true.

blocks.answer: The result of the logical expression is true.

blocks.title: Short-Circuit Evaluation
blocks.text: In logical expressions, short-circuit evaluation means that the second operand is not evaluated if the first operand is sufficient to determine the result. For example, in `false && (x > 0)`, the expression `(x > 0)` is not evaluated because the result is already determined to be false.

points: Operator precedence and associativity determine the order of evaluation in expressions.
Comparison and logical operators are used to build conditions.
Short-circuit evaluation can optimize performance by avoiding unnecessary computations.
